Listen to this article Share Nigerian businesses cannot afford to overlook the cost of poorly managed physical assets. At a time when operating expenses, financing constraints, and competitive pressures demand greater efficiency, companies must pay closer attention to how effectively they use the machinery, equipment, inventory, and other resources already on their books. Acquiring more assets does not necessarily make a business more productive; knowing what it owns, where those assets are and how well they perform may matter just as much. The problem is that asset management remains an underappreciated part of business productivity. While organisations invest in production equipment, computers, vehicles, tools, and inventory, the information needed to manage these resources is not always reliable, accessible, or regularly updated. Records may be scattered across spreadsheets, paper registers, and departmental databases, while the movement, condition, and use of individual assets receive insufficient attention. The result can be misplaced equipment, underused capacity, unnecessary purchases, avoidable downtime, and weak accountability. These are not merely administrative inconveniences. They affect costs, cash flow, and the quality of management decisions. A company that cannot establish what it owns, where it is located, or whether it is being used efficiently may purchase equipment it already has, allow valuable machinery to remain idle, or discover a maintenance problem only after production has been interrupted. Each failure consumes resources that could have been deployed more productively. Nigeria’s difficult operating environment makes these weaknesses particularly expensive. Businesses contend with high borrowing costs, unreliable electricity, infrastructure deficits, and the pressure to preserve margins amid fluctuating input prices. Where replacement equipment is costly or imported components take time to obtain, the consequences of poor asset management can extend beyond the immediate financial loss to delayed production, missed orders, and dissatisfied customers. Better management cannot eliminate these structural constraints, but it can reduce the avoidable costs that businesses impose on themselves. The issue also has implications for capital allocation. Before committing scarce funds to additional equipment, management should establish whether existing assets are being used to their full potential. Idle machinery, duplicated purchases, and poorly distributed equipment can tie up capital that could otherwise support maintenance, staff development, product improvement, or expansion. A reliable asset register, supported by regular physical verification and utilisation reviews, provides a starting point for making these decisions. Technology can strengthen this process. Barcodes and radio-frequency identification (RFID) can help organisations identify assets and record their movement. Mobile devices can make verification easier, while integrated databases and analytics can help managers monitor location, usage, maintenance schedules, and replacement needs. Properly implemented, these tools can reduce dependence on manual record-keeping and give decision-makers a more consistent picture of the resources available to them. However, technology should not be mistaken for a solution in itself. A digital register that contains inaccurate information will not improve accountability, while a tracking system that records movement without prompting corrective action will have limited operational value. Organisations must first establish clear procedures for registering assets, assigning responsibility, authorising transfers, conducting physical checks, and reporting losses or damage. Technology should reinforce these controls, not substitute for them. The same principle applies to maintenance. Organisations that rely mainly on repairs after equipment breaks down risk incurring costs that could have been anticipated. Maintaining accurate records of equipment condition, servicing history, and expected replacement dates can help businesses plan preventive maintenance and reduce unexpected interruptions. The appropriate approach will differ by sector: a manufacturer may prioritise machine availability, a hospital may focus on the location and condition of critical equipment, while a distributor may concentrate on inventory accuracy and the movement of stock. The common requirement is reliable information linked to operational decisions. Businesses must also measure whether improved asset management produces tangible returns. Introducing a tracking platform or digitising a register should not be treated as success in itself. Management should establish baseline figures for asset losses, equipment downtime, inventory discrepancies, maintenance costs, and time spent locating equipment. It can then set targets, assign responsibility, and review results at regular intervals. The financial case for further investment becomes clearer when organisations can demonstrate reductions in avoidable expenditure or improvements in asset utilisation. Smaller businesses, in particular, need not begin with expensive enterprise-wide systems. A verified asset register, consistent identification labels, designated asset custodians, and scheduled physical checks can establish basic discipline. Digital tools can then be introduced according to the organisation’s size, operational complexity, and demonstrated needs. The priority should be to solve a defined business problem rather than purchase technology because digital transformation has become a fashionable corporate objective. There is a wider governance dimension to this challenge. Assets are not always managed well simply because organisations lack technology. Weak internal controls, unclear departmental responsibilities, and inadequate oversight can undermine even sophisticated systems. Boards and senior management should therefore treat asset management as part of financial control and operational risk management. Regular reconciliation of physical assets with accounting records, documented approval for transfers and disposals, and independent verification where appropriate can help close the gap between what an organisation reports owning and what it can actually account for. Nigeria’s productivity debate often focuses on access to capital, infrastructure, skills, and new technology. These priorities are justified, but the efficient use of existing resources deserves equal attention. Businesses cannot control every external cost, yet they can improve the quality of their own operational decisions. Better asset management is one practical way to do so. Ultimately, competitive advantage will not depend solely on how much equipment a business acquires or how much it spends on digital systems. It will also depend on whether management can account for its resources, keep them in service, deploy them where they are most productive, and determine when replacement or expansion is justified. For ChamsAccess Limited, the broader business imperative is to help organisations turn asset visibility into better operational decisions. For Nigerian businesses facing persistent cost pressures, that discipline is not a peripheral administrative concern. It is part of the work of building more productive, accountable, and resilient enterprises.
